solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Complicated logic I use to preserve previous purpose for Apple

indicators.note: complicated letters are tangled up
the anagram keeps the other piece inside it, as a jar preserves fruit

parts.note: previous = OLD, purpose = END (an end in view)

explanation.surface: Someone untangling the reasoning behind an Apple product, or the company's old mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A makes Apple look like the tech company; it is the fruit, and the Golden Delicious is a variety of apple.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden Delicious is a well-known variety of apple.

clue.text: Finally snap in rage, so agitated

definitions.text: Finally snap in rage, so agitated

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its last letter is used
stirred-up letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who has held it together until they finally snap in a fit of rage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: it builds the letters and also describes what it means to go spare, British slang for losing your temper.
explanation.definitionFit: To go spare is British slang for becoming furious, exactly finally snapping in agitated rage.

clue.text: Fencing's bound to fall quickly if uncapped

indicators.note: with its cap, the top letter, taken off

parts.note: to fall quickly = PLUNGE, minus its first letter P

explanation.surface: A claim that a fencing sport is doomed to decline fast if the protective tips come off the blades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'certain to', but here it is a leap, and ''s' belongs to the definition, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunge is the forward thrust in fencing, a sudden bound at the opponent.

clue.text: Add detail to meme's content, like Clangers?

indicators.note: a word's content is what sits inside it

explanation.surface: Adding a flourish to an internet meme about the Clangers, a British children's TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Clangers were knitted creatures in a 1970s British children's programme; here the word just means things that clang, so bells, and 'like' them is BELL-ISH.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to embellish is to decorate, so adding ornamental detail to a tale or design.

clue.text: Day journal is a tedious thing

parts.note: a rag is a newspaper, usually a poor one

explanation.surface: A grumble that keeping a daily diary is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day journal' reads as a diary; split it, and 'journal' is a newspaper, which crosswords love to call a rag.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a drag is a bore, anything that drags on.

clue.text: Sample of polite, rational, educated people

indicators.note: a sample is a small part taken from the words that follow

explanation.surface: A survey drawing on polite, rational, educated respondents.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma hides the join: the answer runs across 'polite' and 'rational'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the learned classes, from Latin for lettered men.

clue.text: Maximum quota for fattened fowl

parts.note: a cap is an upper limit
on = for, as in a limit on something

explanation.surface: A limit on how many fattened birds a farmer may produce.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'a maximum quota for' is simply 'a cap on', and the two words run together into the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel fattened for the table.

clue.text: Prominent bust or bum one has

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means bad or faulty, so the letters are wrong

explanation.surface: A comment on whichever body part sticks out most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a body part to pair with 'bust'; it is the adjective meaning dud, telling you to rearrange BUST OR. 'One has' is spoken as I'VE, one being I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obtrusive sticks out, prominent in an unwelcome way.

clue.text: Multitudes uprising advance endlessly as rich loaf

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read bottom to top
a word without an end has lost its last letter

parts.note: advance (money) = LEND, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Crowds rise up to share out a rich loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Stollen is a German fruit bread eaten at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Stollen is a rich fruit loaf, often with marzipan inside.

clue.text: Roughly clean both sides of scab after the rest

parts.note: the two sides of Scab are S and B, written S AND B

indicators.note: the two outside letters of scab

parts.note: last = coming after all the rest

explanation.surface: Cleaning a wound's scab once everything else has been dealt with.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to write out 'both sides' in full: the sides are S and B, and the AND itself goes into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To sandblast is to clean a surface by blasting sand at it, a rough cleaning.

clue.text: Terrace with partial occupation

indicators.note: only part of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A terrace, perhaps of houses, that is only partly lived in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrace' suggests a row of houses to go with 'occupation'; here it is paving outside one.
explanation.definitionFit: A patio is a paved terrace beside a house.

clue.text: Ancient nameless ruin of Donegal

indicators.note: without N, the abbreviation for name
ruined letters are knocked into a new shape

explanation.surface: An old, forgotten ruin in County Donegal, in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin' looks like a noun for the old building in the scene; it is the instruction to wreck the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something age-old is ancient, having existed for ages.

clue.text: Composed question in letter from Athens, enveloped with scent

parts.note: a scent is the trail a hound follows

indicators.note: the scent wraps around what came before

explanation.surface: A calmly written question in a perfumed letter posted from Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'letter from Athens' is not correspondence but an alphabet letter, and 'scent' is the hound's sense of the word, the line it follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Composed and tranquil both mean calm and untroubled.

clue.text: Latecomer in election takes the lead, sounding repetitive

indicators.note: the last letter moves to the front

parts.words: Latecomer in election takes the lead
parts.note: election = CHOICE; its latecomer is its last letter, which goes to the front
election = choice, now without the E that moved up

explanation.surface: A late-declaring candidate surges ahead in an election, repeating the same lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latecomer' is not a candidate but the last letter of CHOICE; move E to the front and CHOICE becomes ECHOIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoic means imitating or repeating a sound, like an echo.

clue.text: Deeply experienced judge abandoned over time

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down

explanation.surface: A seasoned judge who was deserted long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deeply experienced' reads as 'very seasoned', which sits with the judge; it means deeply felt.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartfelt means felt deeply, and to experience is to feel, so deeply experienced is a fair paraphrase.

clue.text: One taking place at back of stable?

definitions.text: One taking place at back of stable?

indicators.note: being at the back of something means coming after it

parts.note: a stall is a stable compartment
on = happening, as in 'the show is on'

explanation.surface: A horse settling into its place at the back of the stable.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue simply describes the horse in its stable, so the wordplay and the definition are the same sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse, just the sort of one kept at the back of a stable.

clue.text: Some underwear in pine bathrooms

parts.note: to pine is to long for
john is American slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: Underwear left lying in bathrooms fitted out in pine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the wood of the bathroom fittings; it is the verb, to long.
explanation.definitionFit: Long johns are full-length thermal underpants.

clue.text: Net weight nonstandard beer tin holds

indicators.note: not in the standard order, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A label complaint: the net weight of this odd-sized beer can is not what it says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net weight' is a phrase from packaging; split it, and 'Net' is the internet, jokily called the interweb.
explanation.definitionFit: Interweb is a jokey name for the internet, the Net.

clue.text: Try to poach bananas and the centre nearly splits

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go mad
nearly means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

parts.note: centre = HUB, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A kitchen disaster: poaching bananas until the middle splits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poach' suggests cooking and 'bananas' fruit; poach means lure staff away, and bananas is crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To headhunt is to try to poach staff from another firm.

clue.text: Indifferent writer saying one could cut lead

parts.note: a hack is a mediocre writer
a saw is an old saying

explanation.surface: A mediocre writer claiming that one person could take the leading role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' reads as the leading role; it is the metal, which a hacksaw cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw for cutting metal, such as lead.

clue.text: Bearing north, take advantage of graphic directions as a turn-off

definitions.note: 'a turn-off' is a noun; read 'as a turn-off' as describing something off-putting, which is adjectival

parts.note: to use someone is to take advantage of them
x and y are the two directions on a graph

explanation.surface: Heading north to exploit explicit instructions, which prove off-putting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graphic' hints at explicit content, fitting the sexy theme; it means belonging to a graph, whose axes run x and y.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition read as 'being a turn-off' describes something off-putting, which is what unsexy means.

clue.text: Vote for split when accounts are concluded?

parts.note: yea is a vote in favour
to rend is to split apart

explanation.surface: A vote to split up at the moment the books are closed.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (4,3) invites YEAR + END; the wordplay breaks the letters at a different point.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by the question mark: closing the books is the most familiar thing that happens at the year end.

clue.text: Made Urban withdraw to make jerk godly?

indicators.note: drawing back, the letters are read backwards

parts.note: make godly = DEIFY, jerk = TIC: deify a tic

explanation.surface: Pope Urban backing away from turning a fool into a god.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital U makes Urban look like a pope; it is just the adjective. Deify the tic, then read the whole thing backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cityfied means made urban, turned into or adapted to city life.

clue.text: Unpreserved meat has changed hands

parts.note: left becomes right: L swaps for R

explanation.surface: Meat that has been sold on without being cured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changed hands' sounds like a sale; here the hands are left and right, L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh food has not been preserved by salting, drying or tinning.

clue.text: When I'm due in Paris I roughly pack things thrown out

explanation.surface: A traveller heading for Paris packing things roughly and throwing some out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When I'm due' is a travel abbreviation, estimated time of arrival, and 'roughly' is the Latin circa shortened to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical plural, used mainly of volcanic material or of matter blasted from a star.

clue.text: Mufflers with ends trimmed cut into figure, possibly

indicators.note: both end letters are cut off

parts.note: mufflers = SCARVES, minus S and S

explanation.surface: Scarves trimmed at the ends and cut to flatter the figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like a body shape to go with scarves; it is a statue you might carve.
explanation.definitionFit: To carve is to cut material into a figure, such as a statue.

clue.text: Root is immature insect food
Podcaster's influenced kid

indicators.note: a podcaster speaks, so this is what you hear

explanation.surface: A podcast host has swayed a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' reads as a child being influenced; it is kid leather, goatskin, and suede is another soft leather.
explanation.definitionFit: Kid is soft goatskin leather, and suede is similar soft napped leather, often kid.

clue.text: Toiler's poorer when accommodating old king, King Henry

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the physics unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A labourer is worse off for having to put up the old king, Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Henry' looks like one monarch; it is two abbreviations, K and H, the henry being a unit in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: A workhorse is someone who does a lot of hard toil.

clue.text: Have a wee one after having a wee one?

definitions.text: Have a wee one after having a wee one?

parts.note: the surface pushes a trip to the toilet; the setter means have a wee (Scots: small) drink
the second wee one is a newborn baby

explanation.surface: A trip to the toilet after something small, or a small drink after a birth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a wee one' suggests a toilet visit; the first is a wee dram, the second a wee (Scots for small) baby. To wet the baby's head is the British custom of drinking to a newborn.
explanation.definitionFit: Wetting the baby's head means having a celebratory drink after a baby is born.
